```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4)
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
series <- function(x, f = num, ...) {
  x <- trimws(f(x, ...))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), " and ", x[length(x)])
}
# The files beside this article: the fit of the schools, the runs that it is
# compared with, the contrasts under other assumptions about the classes,
# and the table of the simulation. data-raw/star.R, data-raw/class-size.R
# and data-raw/benchmark/schools.R in the source repository write them. The
# fit, the runs and the table are read in visible chunks, where they are
# first used.
first_stage <- readRDS("class-size-first-stage.rds")
```

This case study analyzes a multisite trial with bayesEfron, from the
students' test scores to what we would report. A multisite trial runs one
experiment in many places, which the package calls sites, so it can tell
us more than whether the treatment works on average. @raudenbush2015 name
three things to learn about the site effects: their mean, how much they
vary, and the effect at each site. bayesEfron estimates all three from
one estimate and one standard error for each site, as
`vignette("bayesEfron")` describes. We follow them through a large
experiment in education, and end up less sure of the second than a first
look at the fit suggests.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

Tennessee's Project STAR assigned students and teachers at random, within
each of 79 schools, to small classes or to regular classes, the regular
ones with or without a teacher's aide. The design called for 13 to 17
students in a small class and 22 to 25 in a regular one
[@achilles2008; @finn1990]. Students in small classes did better on
average. Published analyses disagree about whether they did better by the
same amount in every school: @nye2000 concluded that the effects were
quite consistent across schools, whereas @konstantopoulos2011 concluded
that they varied significantly across schools in every grade. We use the
data from kindergarten, the first of the experiment's four years.

## From students to one estimate for each school

To fit the model we need an estimate and a standard error for each
school, not the students' scores, so we first have to compute them. A
multisite trial adds this step to a meta-analysis, where both are taken
from published reports. The data set `star_schools` has the result, and
we print the first rows of some of its columns.

```{r data}
head(star_schools[, c("site", "location", "yi", "sei", "n_students",
                      "n_classes", "n_classes_small")])
```

`yi` is the difference between a school's small classes and its regular
classes, with or without an aide, in a composite of the reading and
mathematics scores at the end of kindergarten. Its unit is the standard
deviation of the composite among the students who have both scores. `sei`
is its standard error, the subject of the rest of this section. See
`?star_schools` for the source of the data.

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
schools <- star_schools
small <- table(schools$n_classes_small)
source <- attr(schools, "source")
ratio <- schools$sei / schools$sei_ols
one <- schools$n_classes_small == 1L
two <- schools$n_classes_small == 2L
stopifnot(
  nrow(schools) == 79L, sum(schools$n_students) == 5786L,
  sum(schools$n_classes) == 325L, sum(schools$n_classes_small) == 127L,
  round(mean(schools$n_students)) == 73,
  sum(schools$n_classes >= 3L & schools$n_classes <= 5L) > 65L,
  small[["1"]] == 35L, small[["2"]] == 41L, sum(small) - 76L == 3L,
  all(ratio > 1), stats::median(ratio) > 1.85, stats::median(ratio) < 1.95,
  max(schools$sei[two]) < min(schools$sei[one]),
  abs(source$class_sd - 0.34) < 0.01, abs(source$residual_sd - 0.83) < 0.01,
  stats::cor(schools$yi, schools$yi_ols) > 0.99,
  # The file of the other assumptions starts from the same contrasts.
  identical(first_stage$class_sd, source$class_sd),
  first_stage$between_class_df == 167L
)
print(c(range(schools$sei[one]), range(schools$sei[two]), stats::median(ratio)))
```

In all, the sample has 5,786 students in 325 classes, which is a lot for
the mean effect but not much for any one school. A school has
`r round(mean(schools$n_students))` students on average, and most schools
have 3 to 5 classes: `r small[["1"]]` schools have a single small class,
and `r small[["2"]]` have two.

Classes matter because students in the same class have the same teacher
and the same room, so their scores are alike for reasons that have
nothing to do with the size of the class. In a school with one small
class, the difference between that class and the others is also the
difference between one teacher and the others. A standard error that
treats the students as independent ignores this. The mixed model below
takes it into account. It has an intercept and a small-class contrast for
each school and a random intercept for each class, and it is fitted to
all the schools at once with the lme4 package [@bates2015].

```{r first-stage, eval = FALSE}
# One row for each student: the composite `y`, the indicator `small`, and
# factors for the school and the class.
model <- lme4::lmer(y ~ 0 + school + school:small + (1 | class),
                    data = students)
```

The 79 coefficients of `school:small` are the estimates in `yi`, and
`sei` has their standard errors. In the source repository, the script
`data-raw/star.R` builds `star_schools` in this way from the public data
file. The mixed model estimates a standard deviation of
`r num(source$class_sd)` between classes of the same kind in a school and
of `r num(source$residual_sd)` between the students of a class.

Because these two numbers are common to all the schools, a school's
standard error is determined by the number and sizes of its small and
regular classes. It is between `r num(min(schools$sei[one]))` and
`r num(max(schools$sei[one]))` for the schools with one small class, and
between `r num(min(schools$sei[two]))` and `r num(max(schools$sei[two]))`
for the schools with two. Another column, `sei_ols`, is the standard
error that ordinary least squares (OLS) gives the same contrast within a
school, with the students treated as independent. It is smaller for every
school, and for the median school the standard error from the mixed model
is `r num(stats::median(ratio), 1)` times as large.

Like other analyses of this kind, the model that we fit next treats the
standard errors as known. Here they depend on the variance between
classes, which is estimated with `r first_stage$between_class_df` degrees
of freedom (the number of classes minus the number of groups of classes
of the same kind in a school), and on the
assumption that this variance is the same for small and regular classes
and in every school. We come back to both in the section on the standard
errors.

## A fit with one remaining warning

We fit the model with the call below. It sets four sampler arguments, and
most of this section explains why.

```{r fit-call, eval = FALSE}
fit <- bayes_efron_fit(star_schools, seed = 1985, adapt_delta = 0.99,
                       max_treedepth = 12, iter_warmup = 2000,
                       iter_sampling = 6000)
```

We ran this call in advance and saved the fit, thinned to 1 draw in 30.
The next chunk reads it from a file beside the source of this article.

```{r fit}
fit <- readRDS("class-size-fit.rds")
fit
```

The output has a `Warnings` line, which lists `ebfmi`, the E-BFMI
diagnostic of the sampler.

The four arguments are a response to what the defaults did with these
data. To show this, we ran `bayes_efron_fit(star_schools)` with 6 different
seeds, and then the call above with the same seeds. The diagnostics and
summaries of these 12 runs are in `evidence`, a list of results that we
computed in advance for this article. We read it and print the runs with
the defaults.

```{r runs-defaults}
evidence <- readRDS("class-size-evidence.rds")
runs <- evidence$runs
show_runs <- function(x) {
  data.frame(seed = x$seed, ebfmi_min = round(x$ebfmi_min, 2),
             max_rhat = round(x$max_rhat, 3),
             min_ess_bulk = round(x$min_ess_bulk),
             divergences = x$divergences, treedepth_hits = x$treedepth_hits,
             mean_g = round(x$mean_g, 3), sd_g = round(x$sd_g, 3))
}
show_runs(runs[runs$setting == "defaults", ])
```

```{r runs-facts, include = FALSE}
default <- runs[runs$setting == "defaults", ]
stored <- runs[runs$setting == "stored", ]
d <- diagnose(fit)
this <- stored[stored$seed == 1985, ]
stopifnot(
  nrow(default) == 6L, nrow(stored) == 6L, identical(default$seed, stored$seed),
  # The stored fit is the first row of its table.
  abs(this$ebfmi_min - min(d$ebfmi)) < 1e-12, this$max_rhat == max(d$rhat, na.rm = TRUE),
  identical(d$sampler_diagnostics_warned, "ebfmi"),
  length(d$sampler_diagnostics_failed) == 0L,
  isTRUE(attr(fit$metadata, "storage")$thin == 30L),
  # The defaults: a low E-BFMI in every run, the tree depth in five, a
  # divergent transition in one.
  all(default$ebfmi_min < 0.3), sum(default$treedepth_hits > 0) == 5L,
  sum(default$divergences > 0) == 1L,
  # The settings of the stored fit.
  all(stored$ebfmi_min < 0.3), all(stored$divergences == 0),
  all(stored$max_rhat < 1.01), all(stored$min_ess_bulk > 1100),
  all(stored$min_ess_tail > 1100), sum(stored$treedepth_hits > 0) == 2L,
  max(stored$treedepth_hits) <= 5L,
  # The summaries over the twelve runs.
  all(round(runs$mean_g, 3) %in% c(0.204, 0.205)),
  diff(range(runs$sd_g)) < 0.01, diff(range(runs$sd_g_lower)) < 0.015,
  diff(range(runs$sd_g_upper)) < 0.015,
  # The same schools with the smaller standard errors.
  evidence$ols$run$ebfmi_min > 0.6, evidence$ols$run$warned == "",
  evidence$ols$run$failed == ""
)
print(range(runs$sd_g)); print(range(runs$sd_g_lower)); print(range(runs$sd_g_upper))
```

In every run at least one chain has an E-BFMI below 0.3 (`ebfmi_min` is
the smallest of the 4 chains). In 5 of the 6 runs some iterations reach
the maximum tree depth, and one run has a divergent transition, which
`diagnose()` counts as a failed check. `vignette("diagnostics")` gives
the remedies:

- a higher `adapt_delta` (a smaller step size) for divergent transitions,
- a higher `max_treedepth` for iterations at the maximum tree depth,
- a longer run (`iter_warmup` and `iter_sampling`) for effective sample
  sizes or an R-hat near their thresholds.

The four arguments in our call apply all three. In `runs` these settings
are labeled `"stored"`, and the same 6 seeds now give the following.

```{r runs-stored}
show_runs(runs[runs$setting == "stored", ])
```

No run has a divergent transition, every R-hat is below 1.01, and the
smallest effective sample size is above 1,100. In 2 runs a few iterations
still reach the maximum tree depth, at most
`r max(stored$treedepth_hits)` of 24,000. But the E-BFMI stays below 0.3
in every run, with either setting.

A low E-BFMI means that the chains move slowly between the high and the
low levels of the log density, as `vignette("diagnostics")` explains. It
is a warning about how well the sampler explores, and it is there in all
12 runs. What we can check is whether the results depend on the run. Over
the 12 runs the mean of $g$, the distribution of the effects, is
`r num(min(runs$mean_g), 3)` or `r num(max(runs$mean_g), 3)`, its
standard deviation is between `r num(min(runs$sd_g), 3)` and
`r num(max(runs$sd_g), 3)`, and each limit of the 90% interval for that
standard deviation varies by less than 0.015. So the summaries are stable
across seeds and settings. That does not show that the sampler has
explored all of the posterior distribution, and a report of the fit
should say that the warning was there.

When the same 79 schools are given the OLS standard errors, which are
about half as large, the warning is not there: a fit with the defaults
then has an E-BFMI of `r num(evidence$ols$run$ebfmi_min)` and no warning
of any kind. The simulation below shows which data sets of this design
have the warning and which do not.

## The mean and the spread of the effects

We plot the estimate of $g$ with `plot_g()`, and add marks for the 79
estimates and, as a dashed curve, the normal model fitted to them by
restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

```{r g-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "The estimated density of the 79 effects, a single peak near 0.2 with a 90% band, a dashed normal curve that nearly coincides with it, and marks for the estimates, which spread from about -0.9 to 1.4."}
plot_g(fit, observed = "rug", normal = TRUE)
```

The two curves nearly coincide. For the numbers we use `confint()` with
`type = "g"`, which gives the mean, the variance and the standard
deviation of $g$, each with a 90% interval.

```{r g}
confint(fit, type = "g")
```

```{r g-facts, include = FALSE}
g_ci <- confint(fit, type = "g")
rownames(g_ci) <- g_ci$parameter
normal <- evidence$normal
rownames(normal) <- normal$standard_errors
reml <- normal["classes", ]
grid <- d$grid
negative <- g_summary(fit, type = "prob", upper = 0)
stopifnot(
  abs(g_ci["mean_g", "mean"] - reml$mean) < 0.01, g_ci["mean_g", "lower"] > 0.1,
  g_ci["sd_g", "mean"] > 1.3 * reml$sd, g_ci["sd_g", "lower"] > 0.05,
  reml$df == 78L, reml$p > 0.3, reml$p < 0.4,
  abs(grid$sd_g[["mean"]] - g_ci["sd_g", "mean"]) < 1e-8,
  grid$sd_g_prior[["q50"]] > 1.2, grid$sd_g_prior[["q5"]] > 1,
  negative$mean > 0.08, negative$mean < 0.15, negative$lower < 0.02,
  negative$upper > 0.2
)
print(reml); print(negative)
```

We estimate the mean of the effects at `r num(g_ci["mean_g", "mean"])`
standard deviations of the composite, with a 90% interval from
`r num(g_ci["mean_g", "lower"])` to `r num(g_ci["mean_g", "upper"])`, and
the normal model puts it at `r num(reml$mean)` as well. This is the
part of the answer that the data determine well.

The same cannot be said of the spread. For the standard deviation of $g$
the fit gives `r num(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"])`, with an interval from
`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "lower"])` to `r num(g_ci["sd_g", "upper"])`. The
REML estimate is `r num(reml$sd)`. The test of homogeneity that goes
with the normal model does not reject: its statistic is
`r num(reml$q, 1)` on `r reml$df` degrees of freedom, a p-value of
`r num(reml$p)`.

It is tempting to read the first of these numbers as a finding that the
effect differs from school to school by about 0.2. The interval does
exclude zero, but it could not include it: $g$ is a smooth density on the
grid, so its standard deviation is positive whatever the data are.
`diagnose()` puts the number in context: its `grid` component has this
standard deviation (`sd_g`) beside its prior distribution on the same
grid (`sd_g_prior`).

```{r prior}
diagnose(fit)$grid[c("sd_g", "sd_g_prior")]
```

On this grid the standard deviation of $g$ is about
`r num(grid$sd_g_prior[["q50"]], 1)` before the data and
`r num(grid$sd_g[["mean"]], 1)` after them. So the data have moved it
most of the way toward zero, but we cannot learn from the fit itself how
much further the model would let it go. The same is true of what follows
from the spread, such as the proportion of schools in which small classes
do harm, which `g_summary()` gives as the probability that $g$ puts below
zero.

```{r negative}
g_summary(fit, type = "prob", upper = 0)
```

The fit puts this proportion at `r pct(negative$mean)`, with a 90%
interval from `r pct(negative$lower, 1)` to `r pct(negative$upper)`. To
learn how to read numbers like these, we turn to simulated data, for
which the true spread is known.

## Simulating trials like this one

We simulated data sets with the 79 standard errors of these schools. In
every case the true effects have the mean that REML estimates for the
schools, and their spread follows one of four cases:

- no variation, so that every school has the same effect,
- normal, with the REML estimate of the standard deviation
  (`r num(reml$sd)`),
- normal, with the posterior mean of the standard deviation of $g$
  (`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "mean"])`),
- normal, with the upper limit of the 90% interval for that standard
  deviation (`r num(g_ci["sd_g", "upper"])`).

We drew 200 data sets for each case and fitted each of them twice with
`bayes_efron_fit()`, with the sampler settings of the second section and
with the defaults. We also fitted the normal model by REML and then took
its mean and standard deviation as known, which is a plug-in analysis.

We read the summary of the simulation from a file. The first table is
about the spread of the effects, for the fits
with the settings of the second section (`bayesEfron`) and the plug-in
normal model (`normal`).

```{r simulation}
sims <- read.csv("class-size-samples.csv", check.names = FALSE)
shown <- sims[sims$method %in% c("bayesEfron", "normal"), ]
data.frame(effects = shown$scenario, analysis = shown$method,
           sd = round(shown$sd_mean, 2), sd_q05 = round(shown$sd_q05, 2),
           sd_q95 = round(shown$sd_q95, 2), sd_zero = shown$sd_zero,
           sd_inclusion = shown$sd_inclusion)
```

```{r simulation-facts, include = FALSE}
scenarios <- c("no variation", "normal, SD 0.14", "normal, SD 0.20", "normal, SD 0.35")
cell <- function(method, column, which = scenarios) {
  rows <- sims[sims$method == method, ]
  rows <- rows[match(which, rows$scenario), ]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(rows$scenario))
  rows[[column]]
}
own <- function(column, ...) cell("bayesEfron", column, ...)
defaults <- function(column, ...) cell("bayesEfron, defaults", column, ...)
plug_in <- function(column, ...) cell("normal", column, ...)
known <- function(column) cell("known g", column, scenarios[-1])
observed <- sims$observed_own_sd[1]
as_small <- 1 - own("own_as_large")
all_draws <- runs$sd_g[runs$setting == "stored" & runs$seed == 1985]
stopifnot(
  identical(unique(sims$scenario), scenarios), all(sims$replications == 200),
  abs(observed - g_ci["sd_g", "mean"]) < 1e-6,
  # The same comparison with the value from all the draws of the stored call.
  all_draws < observed, observed - all_draws < 0.003,
  all(own("own_as_large_all_draws") - own("own_as_large") >= 0),
  all(own("own_as_large_all_draws") - own("own_as_large") < 0.025),
  abs(own("true_sd")[2] - reml$sd) < 1e-6, abs(own("true_sd")[3] - observed) < 1e-6,
  abs(own("true_sd")[4] - g_ci["sd_g", "upper"]) < 0.001,
  # The standard deviation of g: what the fit reports without variation, and
  # how often each distribution gives a value like that of the schools.
  own("sd_mean")[1] > 0.15, own("sd_q05")[1] > 0.1, own("sd_q95")[1] > observed,
  own("own_as_large")[1] > 0.2, own("own_as_large")[1] < 0.3,
  all(diff(own("own_as_large")) > 0), as_small[4] < 0.05,
  own("sd_inclusion")[1] == 0, all(own("sd_inclusion")[2:4] > 0.9),
  plug_in("sd_zero")[1] > 0.4, plug_in("sd_zero")[2] > 0.2,
  # The intervals of the schools.
  own("inclusion")[1] > 0.99, own("inclusion")[2] > 0.9,
  all(own("inclusion")[3:4] < 0.89), all(own("inclusion")[3:4] > 0.87),
  all(own("inclusion_se") < 0.005),
  # The data sets whose fit reports a standard deviation no larger than that
  # of the schools.
  identical(own("sd_as_small"), as.integer(round(200 * as_small))),
  own("inclusion_sd_as_small")[1] > 0.99, own("inclusion_sd_as_small")[2] > 0.9,
  own("inclusion_sd_as_small")[3] < 0.83, own("sd_as_small")[3] > 50,
  all(plug_in("inclusion")[1:3] < 0.8), plug_in("inclusion")[1] < 0.6,
  plug_in("inclusion")[4] < 0.89, all(abs(known("inclusion") - 0.9) < 0.01),
  # The school with the largest estimate.
  all(own("largest_inclusion") > 0.9), all(own("largest_error") > 0.04),
  which.max(own("largest_error")) == 1L, own("largest_error")[1] > 0.12,
  # How many intervals exclude zero when every school has the same effect.
  own("excluding_zero_q05")[1] <= 2, own("excluding_zero_q95")[1] >= 60,
  # The sampler: the two settings.
  all(own("with_divergences") == 0), all(own("ess_below_400") == 0),
  sum(own("rhat_above_1.01")) < 10, sum(defaults("with_divergences")) > 100,
  sum(defaults("rhat_above_1.01")) > 50,
  all(defaults("sd_change_largest") < 0.02),
  all(abs(defaults("inclusion_change")) < 0.001),
  # At most two schools of 79 in any data set.
  max(defaults("inclusion_change_largest")) < 2.5 / 79,
  sum(own("with_treedepth_hits")) > 200,
  # E-BFMI: low when the estimate of g is narrow.
  own("ebfmi_below_0.3")[1] > 180, own("ebfmi_below_0.3")[4] < 30,
  all(diff(own("ebfmi_below_0.3")) < 0), all(own("ebfmi_sd_correlation") > 0.6),
  own("inclusion_ebfmi_below")[3] < own("inclusion_ebfmi_above")[3] - 0.05,
  all(own("end_warnings") == 0)
)
print(rbind(own_sd = own("sd_mean"), as_large = own("own_as_large"),
            inclusion = own("inclusion"), largest = own("largest_error")))
print(rbind(below = own("inclusion_ebfmi_below"), above = own("inclusion_ebfmi_above"),
            correlation = own("ebfmi_sd_correlation")))
```

The columns are as follows.

- `sd` is the estimated standard deviation of the effects, averaged over
  the data sets: the posterior mean of the standard deviation of $g$ for
  bayesEfron, the REML estimate for the normal model.
- `sd_q05` and `sd_q95` are the 5% and 95% quantiles of those estimates.
- `sd_zero` is the proportion of data sets in which the estimate is zero.
- `sd_inclusion` is the coverage of the 90% interval for the standard
  deviation, the proportion of data sets in which it contains the true
  value.

When every school has the same effect, the fit still reports a standard
deviation of `r num(own("sd_mean")[1])` on average, and a value between
`r num(own("sd_q05")[1])` and `r num(own("sd_q95")[1])` in 90% of the
data sets. The value for the real schools, `r num(observed)`, is inside
that range. The column `own_as_large` of the summary is the proportion of
data sets with a posterior mean at least as large as the one for the real
schools.

```{r as-large}
shown <- sims[sims$method == "bayesEfron", ]
data.frame(effects = shown$scenario, own_as_large = shown$own_as_large)
```

A posterior mean that large occurred in
`r pct(own("own_as_large")[1], 1)` of the data sets without any
variation, and in `r series(own("own_as_large")[2:3], pct, 1)` of those
with standard deviations of 0.14 and 0.20. The fit of the 79 schools
therefore does not show that the effect of small classes varies. It does
limit how large the
variation can be: when the true standard deviation was 0.35, a posterior
mean as small as the one for the schools occurred in `r pct(as_small[4], 1)` of the data
sets. These percentages compare the simulated fits with
`r num(observed, 3)`, the posterior mean of the 800 stored draws. If we
compare with `r num(all_draws, 3)`, from all the draws of the same run,
the first three become
`r series(own("own_as_large_all_draws")[1:3], pct, 1)`.

We should read the interval for the standard deviation in the same way.
It contained the true value in
`r series(own("sd_inclusion")[2:4], pct, 1)` of the data sets in the
three normal cases, and in none of those without variation, where its
lower limit was `r num(own("sd_lower_mean")[1])` on average. Its upper
limit can be used, but its lower limit is not evidence against zero. REML
errs in the other direction: it estimates the standard deviation as zero
in `r pct(plug_in("sd_zero")[1], 1)` of the data sets without variation,
and still in `r pct(plug_in("sd_zero")[2], 1)` of those with a standard
deviation of 0.14.

The next table is about the individual schools. It adds the rows called
`known g`, for an analysis that is given the distribution that the
effects come from, which is possible only in a simulation. Without
variation that distribution is the common effect itself, so this case has
no such row.

```{r simulation-schools}
shown <- sims[sims$method != "bayesEfron, defaults", ]
data.frame(effects = shown$scenario, analysis = shown$method,
           inclusion = round(shown$inclusion, 3),
           length = round(shown$length, 2),
           largest_inclusion = shown$largest_inclusion,
           largest_error = round(shown$largest_error, 2))
```

`inclusion` is the coverage of the schools' 90% intervals, that is, the
proportion of the true effects inside them, and `length` is their mean
length. The other two columns follow one school in each data set, the one
with the largest estimate: `largest_inclusion` is how often its interval
covers its true effect, and `largest_error` is the average difference
between its posterior mean and its true effect.

In the four cases the bayesEfron intervals contained
`r series(own("inclusion"), pct, 1)` of the true effects, with Monte
Carlo standard errors below 0.5 percentage points. They are longer than
they need to be when the effects do not vary, and they fall short of the
nominal 90% by `r num(100 * (0.9 - own("inclusion")[3]), 1)` and
`r num(100 * (0.9 - own("inclusion")[4]), 1)` percentage points when the
standard deviation is 0.20 and 0.35. For the plug-in normal model the
intervals contained `r series(plug_in("inclusion"), pct, 1)`, because
that analysis takes its two estimates as known, and where REML estimates
no variation, every interval is a single point.

These percentages are averages over all the data sets of a case, and the
fit of the real schools is not an average one: the standard deviation
that it reports is on the low side for data with a true standard
deviation of 0.20. Among the data sets in which the fit reported a
standard deviation no larger than the one for the real schools
(`r series(own("sd_as_small")[1:3], format)` data sets in the first three
cases), the intervals contained
`r series(own("inclusion_sd_as_small")[1:3], pct, 1)` of the true
effects. When the effects varied with a standard deviation of 0.20 and
the data happened not to show it, the intervals for the schools were too
short.

For the school with the largest estimate in a data set, the posterior
mean was too high on average in all four cases, by
`r num(min(own("largest_error")))` to `r num(max(own("largest_error")))`,
and by the most when the effects did not vary. Its interval contained its
true effect in at least `r pct(min(own("largest_inclusion")))` of the
data sets in every case.

We can also use the simulation to compare the two sampler settings. Under
the settings of the second section, none of the 800 fits had a divergent
transition or a bulk effective sample size below 400,
`r sum(own("rhat_above_1.01"))` had an R-hat above 1.01, and in
`r sum(own("with_treedepth_hits"))` some iterations reached the maximum
tree depth. Under the defaults, `r sum(defaults("with_divergences"))`
fits had divergent transitions and `r sum(defaults("rhat_above_1.01"))`
an R-hat above 1.01. Even so, the summaries barely depended on the
setting. Between the two, the posterior mean of the standard deviation of
$g$ differed by less than 0.02 in every data set, and the proportion of
true effects inside the intervals by less than 0.001 on average and by at
most 2 of the 79 schools in any data set.

As for the E-BFMI, it was below 0.3 in `r own("ebfmi_below_0.3")[1]` of
the 200 fits without variation and in `r own("ebfmi_below_0.3")[4]` of
the 200 with a standard deviation of 0.35. Within each case it was lower
when the estimate of $g$ was narrower: its correlation with the posterior
mean of the standard deviation of $g$ is between
`r num(min(own("ebfmi_sd_correlation")))` and
`r num(max(own("ebfmi_sd_correlation")))`. In these data sets, then, a
low E-BFMI went with a narrow estimate of $g$. We cannot tell from these
runs whether the model could be written so that it samples such data
without the warning. A narrow estimate of $g$ is also the condition under
which the school intervals were too short, and the two show the same
pattern. When the standard deviation was 0.20, the intervals
contained `r pct(own("inclusion_ebfmi_below")[3], 1)` of the true effects
among the fits with a low E-BFMI and
`r pct(own("inclusion_ebfmi_above")[3], 1)` among the others.

## The schools one by one

`plot_sites()` plots the posterior mean and the intervals of every
school, and we order the schools by their estimates.

```{r sites-plot, fig.height = 7.5, fig.alt = "One row for each of the 79 schools, ordered by estimate: the posterior mean with its 50% and 90% intervals, and the estimate as an open circle. The estimates spread from about -0.9 to 1.4, and the posterior means stay close to the dashed line at the mean of the distribution of effects."}
plot_sites(fit, sort_by = "observed")
```

```{r sites-facts, include = FALSE}
sites <- site_summary(fit)
center <- g_ci["mean_g", "mean"]
weight <- (sites$mean - center) / (sites$estimate - center)
positive <- exceedance_prob(fit, threshold = 0)
above <- sum(sites$lower > 0)
raw_length <- mean(2 * stats::qnorm(0.95) * sites$se)
largest <- which.max(sites$estimate)
second <- order(sites$estimate, decreasing = TRUE)[2]
stopifnot(
  identical(sites$estimate, star_schools$yi), above == 15L, sum(sites$upper < 0) == 0L,
  min(sites$mean) > 0, max(sites$mean) < 0.6,
  stats::median(weight) > 0.12, stats::median(weight) < 0.16,
  min(positive) > 0.6, mean(sites$upper - sites$lower) < 0.45 * raw_length,
  largest == 5L, second == 60L, sites$se[second] < sites$se[largest],
  sites$mean[second] > sites$mean[largest], sites$upper[second] > 1.4,
  star_schools$n_classes[second] == 7L, star_schools$n_classes[largest] == 3L,
  # School 60: longer than the interval of its estimate alone, and an upper
  # limit that moves with the draws and with the standard errors.
  sites$upper[second] - sites$lower[second] > 2 * stats::qnorm(0.95) * sites$se[second],
  identical(evidence$full_sites$estimate, star_schools$yi),
  abs(evidence$full_sites$upper[second] - sites$upper[second]) > 0.05,
  abs(evidence$full_sites$upper[largest] - sites$upper[largest]) < 0.02,
  identical(evidence$first_stage$variant, c("common", "lower", "upper", "by_kind")),
  abs(evidence$first_stage$site_60_upper[1] - evidence$full_sites$upper[second]) < 1e-12,
  diff(range(evidence$first_stage$site_60_upper)) > 0.7,
  diff(range(evidence$first_stage$site_5_upper)) > 0.5,
  abs(evidence$first_stage$site_5_upper[1] - evidence$full_sites$upper[largest]) < 1e-12
)
upper_5 <- evidence$first_stage$site_5_upper
upper_60 <- evidence$first_stage$site_60_upper
print(c(range(sites$estimate), range(sites$mean), stats::median(weight), min(positive)))
```

The open circles are the estimates, which run from
`r num(min(sites$estimate))` to `r num(max(sites$estimate))`, and the
points are the posterior means, which run from `r num(min(sites$mean))`
to `r num(max(sites$mean))`. For the median school, the posterior mean
lies `r pct(stats::median(weight))` of the way from the mean of $g$ to
the estimate. On average the 90% intervals have a length of
`r num(mean(sites$upper - sites$lower))`, whereas intervals from the
estimates and their standard errors alone would have a mean length of
`r num(raw_length)`.

`exceedance_prob()` returns the posterior probability that each school's
effect is above a threshold, here zero. We print the range of these
probabilities and count the 90% intervals that lie above zero.

```{r positive}
positive <- exceedance_prob(fit, threshold = 0)
range(positive)
sum(site_summary(fit)$lower > 0)
```

For every school the probability of a positive effect is at least
`r num(floor(100 * min(positive)) / 100)`, and for `r above` schools the 90% interval lies
above zero. These numbers describe schools with a common positive mean
more than they distinguish one school from another. In the simulated data
sets in which every school had the same effect, the number of intervals
that excluded zero was anywhere between `r own("excluding_zero_q05")[1]`
and `r own("excluding_zero_q95")[1]` in 90% of the data sets, depending
on where the mean of the estimates happened to fall.

Schools 5 and 60 have the two largest estimates, and `site_summary()`
returns their rows.

```{r two-schools}
site_summary(fit, sites = c(5, 60))[, c("label", "estimate", "se", "mean",
                                        "lower", "upper")]
```

School 5, with 3 classes, has the largest estimate, which the fit shrinks
to a posterior mean of `r num(sites$mean[largest])`, with an interval
from `r num(sites$lower[largest])` to `r num(sites$upper[largest])`. In
the simulation, the posterior mean of the school with the largest
estimate was too high on average, but its interval contained the true
effect at least as often as its nominal 90%. For a school like this one
we would therefore report the interval.

School 60 has 7 classes and a smaller standard error, and its estimate is
shrunk less. Its posterior distribution has a long right shoulder: the
interval runs from `r num(sites$lower[second])` to
`r num(sites$upper[second])`, and it is longer than the
`r num(2 * stats::qnorm(0.95) * sites$se[second])` of an interval from
the estimate and its standard error alone.

The upper limit of that interval is the least stable number in the fit.
Computed from all the draws of the run instead of the 800 stored ones, it
is `r num(evidence$full_sites$upper[second])`. The upper limits for
both schools also depend on what is assumed about the classes: under the assumptions
compared in the next section, the upper limit for school 5 lies between
`r num(min(upper_5))` and `r num(max(upper_5))`, and the upper limit for
school 60 between `r num(min(upper_60))` and `r num(max(upper_60))`.

## Varying the standard errors

Suppose that we had ignored the classes and analyzed each school by OLS,
with its students treated as independent. We would then fit the model to
the columns `yi_ols` and `sei_ols`.

```{r ols-call, eval = FALSE}
ols <- as_bef_data(star_schools, theta_hat = "yi_ols", sigma = "sei_ols")
fit_ols <- bayes_efron_fit(ols, seed = 1985)
```

The results of this fit are in `evidence$ols`, and
`plot_g()` adds its estimate of $g$ to our plot through the `compare`
argument.

```{r ols-plot, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "Two estimated densities of the 79 effects. The one from the fit above is a narrow peak near 0.2; the one from the fit with the standard errors of ordinary least squares is about twice as wide and half as high."}
ols <- evidence$ols
plot_g(fit, compare = list(
  "OLS standard errors" = data.frame(x = ols$density$value,
                                     density = ols$density$mean)
), xlim = c(-1.5, 2))
```

```{r ols-facts, include = FALSE}
ols_g <- ols$g
rownames(ols_g) <- ols_g$parameter
reml_ols <- normal["OLS", ]
stopifnot(
  ols_g["sd_g", "mean"] > 1.9 * g_ci["sd_g", "mean"],
  ols_g["sd_g", "lower"] > g_ci["sd_g", "mean"],
  abs(ols_g["mean_g", "mean"] - g_ci["mean_g", "mean"]) < 0.02,
  reml_ols$sd > 2 * reml$sd, reml_ols$p < 1e-20,
  ols$intervals_excluding_zero == 26L, sum(ols$sites$upper < 0) == 3L,
  nrow(ols$sites) == 79L, identical(ols$sites$estimate, star_schools$yi_ols)
)
print(ols_g); print(reml_ols)
```

With the OLS standard errors the standard deviation of $g$ is
`r num(ols_g["sd_g", "mean"])`, with an interval from
`r num(ols_g["sd_g", "lower"])` to `r num(ols_g["sd_g", "upper"])`, twice
as large as in the fit above. REML now estimates `r num(reml_ols$sd)`,
the test of homogeneity rejects with a p-value below $10^{-20}$, and
`r ols$intervals_excluding_zero` school intervals exclude zero,
`r sum(ols$sites$upper < 0)` of them on the negative side, compared with
`r above` in the fit above, all on the positive side. The mean of the
effects is almost unchanged, at `r num(ols_g["mean_g", "mean"])`.

Between the two analyses the estimates are almost the same, with a
correlation of `r num(stats::cor(schools$yi, schools$yi_ols), 3)`. It is
the standard errors that differ, because the two analyses answer
different questions. OLS takes the classes that were formed as given, and
its contrast is the difference between those classes. The mixed model
with class intercepts estimates what the difference would be with other
teachers and other classes in the same school, which is what an effect of
class size means. What the smaller standard errors leave out,
the differences between the teachers and the classes of a school, is
counted as variation in the effect of small classes.

We have not reproduced either of the analyses cited at the start, and we
cannot say what part the standard errors play in their disagreement. In our analysis of
one grade, the standard errors that ignore the classes would have shown
strong variation, whereas the standard errors of the fit above, which
take the classes into account, do not show any.

The standard errors that take the classes into account are estimates
too, and we can vary what they depend on in the same way. The results for
four versions of them are in `evidence$first_stage`, labeled in the first
column of the table.

```{r class-variance}
variants <- evidence$first_stage
data.frame(classes = c("one variance", "variance at its lower end",
                       "variance at its upper end", "a variance for each kind"),
           se = round(variants$se_ratio_median, 2),
           reml_sd = round(variants$reml_sd, 2), p = round(variants$p, 3),
           sd_g = round(variants$sd_g, 2), lower = round(variants$sd_g_lower, 2),
           upper = round(variants$sd_g_upper, 2),
           ebfmi_min = round(variants$ebfmi_min, 2))
```

```{r class-variance-facts, include = FALSE}
limits <- first_stage$class_sd_limits
kinds <- first_stage$by_kind
one_step <- first_stage$one_step
stopifnot(
  identical(variants$variant, c("common", "lower", "upper", "by_kind")),
  # The first row is the stored call with all its draws.
  abs(variants$se_ratio_median[1] - 1) < 1e-10, abs(variants$p[1] - reml$p) < 1e-10,
  abs(variants$sd_g[1] - all_draws) < 1e-12,
  limits[["lower"]] < first_stage$class_sd, limits[["upper"]] > first_stage$class_sd,
  limits[["lower"]] > 0.29, limits[["upper"]] < 0.41,
  kinds$sd[["small"]] > 1.3 * kinds$sd[["regular"]], kinds$p < 0.05, kinds$p > 0.01,
  # The lower end: a test that rejects, and no warning about E-BFMI.
  variants$p[2] < 0.05, variants$p[2] > 0.03, variants$ebfmi_min[2] > 0.3,
  !grepl("ebfmi", variants$warned[2]),
  # The upper end and a variance for each kind: no variation by REML.
  all(variants$reml_sd[3:4] == 0), all(variants$p[3:4] > 0.8),
  all(variants$se_ratio_median[3:4] > 1.1), variants$se_ratio_median[2] < 0.92,
  all(variants$failed == ""), all(variants$max_rhat < 1.01),
  all(variants$min_ess_bulk > 400), all(variants$divergences == 0),
  min(variants$sd_g_upper) > 0.3, max(variants$sd_g_upper) < 0.41,
  which.max(variants$sd_g_upper) == 2L,
  one_step$sd > 0.1, one_step$sd < 0.2, one_step$statistic < 1
)
print(limits); print(kinds$sd); print(unlist(one_step))
```

- The first row is the fit of this case study, here with all the draws of
  its run. Its standard errors depend on a standard deviation of
  `r num(first_stage$class_sd)` between classes, with a 95% interval from
  `r num(limits[["lower"]])` to `r num(limits[["upper"]])`.
- In the second and third rows that standard deviation is at the limits
  of the interval.
- In the fourth row the small and the regular classes each have their
  own variance. That mixed model fits the students better, with a
  likelihood-ratio statistic of `r num(kinds$statistic, 1)` on 1 degree
  of freedom (a p-value of `r num(kinds$p)`), and it estimates a standard
  deviation of `r num(kinds$sd[["small"]])` between small classes and
  `r num(kinds$sd[["regular"]])` between regular ones.

`se` is the median over the schools of the ratio of the standard error to
the standard error in the first row. `reml_sd` and `p` are the REML
estimate of the standard deviation of the effects and the p-value of the
test of homogeneity, and the next three columns are the posterior mean
and the 90% interval of the standard deviation of $g$.

When the variance between classes is at the lower end of its interval,
the test of homogeneity rejects at the 5% level, and the fit has no
warning about E-BFMI. Under either of the other two assumptions, REML
estimates no variation at all. The statement that these data do not show
variation therefore fails in one of the four rows, and it depends on a
standard deviation between classes that the data place only between
`r num(limits[["lower"]])` and `r num(limits[["upper"]])`. In every row,
the upper limit of the interval for the standard deviation of the effects
is at most `r num(max(variants$sd_g_upper))`.

We also fitted a model to the students that estimates the variance of the
effect across schools in one step, with the class intercepts of the first
row. It gives a standard deviation of `r num(one_step$sd)` and a
likelihood-ratio statistic of `r num(one_step$statistic)` for the
hypothesis of no variation, which is no evidence against that hypothesis.

For a multisite trial, the two comparisons in this section show where
care is needed. Whether the effect appears to vary depends first on how
the standard errors are computed and on how well the variances behind
them are known, and only then on the model for the distribution of
effects.

## Reporting this trial

The simulation has limits that we should keep in view: one set of 79
standard errors treated as known, normal distributions of the effects,
normal sampling errors, and effects unrelated to their precision. Within
those limits, we would report three things for these schools.

1. The mean effect with its interval, which is the result that the data
   determine well.
2. For the spread, the upper limit of the interval and not the posterior
   mean. The standard deviation of the effects is unlikely to exceed
   `r num(g_ci["sd_g", "upper"])`, or `r num(variants$sd_g_upper[2])`
   with the variance between classes at the lower end of its interval,
   and the data do not show that it differs from zero. In the simulation,
   the model returned a posterior mean between
   `r num(own("sd_mean")[1])` and `r num(own("sd_mean")[3])` on average
   whether the true standard deviation was zero or 0.20.
3. For a school, the interval, with a caution. When the effects varied
   with a standard deviation of 0.20 and the fit reported a standard
   deviation no larger than the one for these schools, the intervals
   contained `r pct(own("inclusion_sd_as_small")[3])` of the true
   effects. The number of intervals that exclude zero tells us nothing
   about the schools.

A report should also say how the standard errors were computed and how
well the variance behind them is known, because the conclusion about the
spread depends on them. And it should say that the sampler issued a
warning, with the checks that were made: several seeds, a longer run, and
a comparison of the summaries.

As in `vignette("teacher-expectancy")`, the plug-in normal model is not
the safer choice. Its intervals for the schools contained
`r series(plug_in("inclusion"), pct, 1)` of the true effects in the four
cases. A normal model that carries the uncertainty in its variance was
not part of our comparison.

Finally, the fit in this article is thinned to 800 of its 24,000 draws.
For a report, run the call at the top of the second section as it is,
which stores every draw.
